scenes.say: An interviewer says: design bit dot ly. You have ten minutes. By the end, you'll answer in five steps with real numbers, then debug a slow endpoint like a senior engineer.

lines.text: Then debug it like a senior.

scenes.say: Today you will do three things. Design bit dot ly with real numbers. Find a slow step with a trace. Fix it, then verify.
lines: Find a slow step with a trace

scenes.title: Design bit.ly
scenes.statement: Design a URL shortener: create short links, and redirect each one to its long URL.

example.input: 100M new links a month, reads 100x writes

scenes.say: Here is the problem. Design a short link service. For example, a hundred million new links a month, and reads a hundred times writes. We want a design in ten minutes.

scenes.head: A coat check ticket
scenes.say: Think of a coat check. You hand over a huge coat, and get a small ticket. Later, you show the ticket and get the coat back. The coat is the long U R L. The ticket is the short code.

scenes.head: Five steps you can repeat
scenes.say: Use five steps. Numbers first. Then the short code. Then the boxes. Then the read path. Then scale and trade-offs.
Your turn. Step one is numbers. A hundred million new links a month, and a month has about two and a half million seconds. About how many writes per second? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 100M links a month ÷ 2.6M seconds. Writes per second?

scenes.head: Back-of-envelope numbers
scenes.say: About forty. A hundred million divided by two and a half million seconds is forty writes a second. Reads are a hundred times more: four thousand a second. Five years is six billion links. At five hundred bytes each, that's three terabytes.

scenes.head: Numbers make decisions
scenes.say: These numbers make the decisions. Forty writes a second? One primary is plenty. Four thousand reads? Cache the hot links, add replicas. Three terabytes? One database to start. Sharding before doing this math is the classic mistake.

scenes.title: Short codes
scenes.statement: Turn a database row id into a short, unique code.
scenes.say: New problem. Turn a row id into a short, unique code. For example, row id one twenty five. We want the code two, one. Seven characters at most.

scenes.head: More symbols, shorter codes
scenes.say: Think of a combination lock. Ten digits per wheel is ten options. Add lowercase letters, and it's thirty six. Add uppercase, and each wheel has sixty two. Seven wheels of sixty two: three and a half trillion codes.

scenes.head: Row 125 becomes code 21
scenes.say: Take row id one twenty five. Divide by sixty two: two, remainder one. The remainder is the last character, one. Two is below sixty two, so it's the first character. The code is two, one.

scenes.head: Base 62 in Python
scenes.say: In code, the alphabet is digits, then lowercase, then uppercase. Divmod gives quotient and remainder. Each remainder becomes a character, put in front. One twenty five prints two, one. The biggest seven character code is all capital Z.

panels.code:
ALPHABET = string.digits + string.ascii_letters
def encode(n):
    s = ""
    while n:
        n, r = divmod(n, 62)
        s = ALPHABET[r] + s
    return s or "0"
print(encode(125), encode(62**7 - 1))

scenes.say: Your turn. We'll store six billion links in five years. How many codes fit in just six characters? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: How many codes fit in 6 base-62 characters?

scenes.head: Counter or random code?
scenes.say: About fifty seven billion. Seven characters leaves room to spare. Counter or random? Collisions: a counter never collides, random needs a check and retry. Guessable: counter codes are sequential, random ones are not. The catch: one counter is a bottleneck, so hand each server a range of ids.
rows: one counter: hand out id ranges

scenes.title: Redirect fast
scenes.statement: Serve 4,000 redirects a second quickly, and still be able to count every click.
scenes.say: New problem. Redirects must be fast. For example, a browser asks for slash twenty one, four thousand times a second. We want the long U R L back in milliseconds. And every click must be countable.

scenes.head: Database reads per second
scenes.say: Reads outnumber writes a hundred to one. That's four thousand reads a second. Popular links repeat, so assume nine in ten are cache hits. Only four hundred reach the database.

scenes.head: The read path
scenes.say: The browser asks the app servers for slash twenty one. The server checks the cache first. Most reads hit there. On a miss, it reads the database, indexed by code. Then it replies with a redirect to the long U R L.

scenes.head: What the redirect looks like
scenes.say: A real handler would look up the code first. Here the URL is fixed. Three oh two means found, go here. The Location header holds the long U R L. Curl shows what the browser sees.
Your turn. A short link answers with three oh one, moved permanently. One user clicks it five times. How many clicks does your server see? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Short link uses 301. One user clicks it 5 times. Server sees?

scenes.head: 301 vs 302
scenes.say: Usually one. Browsers cache a three oh one, and skip your server next time. Browser: three oh one is cached, three oh two is asked again. Analytics: three oh one misses repeat clicks. Use: three oh two when you need counts.

scenes.head: Step 5: when it grows
scenes.say: Now scale. Reads dominate, so cache and add replicas. If one database gets too big, shard by a hash of the code. If the counter is busy, hand out id ranges. Abuse? Rate limit and expire old links.

scenes.head: Follow-ups they ask
scenes.say: Same long U R L twice? Store both, or look up and reuse the code. Custom alias? The unique index rejects a clash. Click analytics? Log each click to a queue, and count it asynchronously.
rows: store both, or look up and reuse
log to a queue, count async

scenes.title: Checkout is slow
scenes.statement: The pager says checkout is slow. Find the cause with evidence, not guesses.

example.output: cause found, p99 back to 150 ms

scenes.say: New problem. It's two in the morning and checkout is slow. For example, p ninety nine is two seconds. We want the cause, and p ninety nine back to a hundred fifty milliseconds. The average looks fine.

scenes.head: Think of a doctor
scenes.say: Don't guess. A doctor checks vitals first, then the history, then orders a scan. Production has the same three: metrics, logs, and traces.
Your turn. A hundred requests came in. Ninety eight took one hundred twenty milliseconds. Two took two seconds each. What was the average response time? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 98 requests at 120 ms, 2 at 2,000 ms. Average?

scenes.head: Average vs p99
scenes.say: About one fifty eight, so the dashboard looks fine. Now sort the times. The p ninety nine is the time ninety nine percent of requests finish within. Here it's two thousand. One user in fifty waits two seconds. The average hides them.

scenes.head: Same data, three numbers
scenes.say: Look at all three. The median is one twenty. The average is one fifty eight. The p ninety nine is two thousand. So alert on percentiles.

scenes.title: Which step is slow?
scenes.statement: Metrics say checkout is slow. Find the one step that eats the time.
scenes.say: Next problem. Metrics say it's slow. For example, one request takes two thousand milliseconds. We want the one step that eats the time. Then we fix it, and verify.

scenes.head: A trace of POST /checkout
scenes.say: A trace says where, timing each step. Here, two thousand milliseconds in total. Auth takes twenty. J S O N takes a hundred. But one S Q L query takes eighteen hundred.

scenes.head: Ask the database for its plan
scenes.say: Ask the database to explain its plan. Before: SCAN. It reads every row to find one user. An index works like a book's index: jump to the page, don't read every page. After creating one, the plan says SEARCH using the index.

panels.label: before
after

output.text:
SCAN orders
SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_user (user_id=?)

scenes.say: Your turn. A different trace: two hundred queries, nine milliseconds each, about eighteen hundred in total. Would an index be the best fix? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: 200 queries at 9 ms each. Best fix?

scenes.head: Symptom to cause
scenes.say: Join or batch them. Each query is already fast. Many small queries: N plus one. One query for the orders, then one per order. One slow query: a missing index, so read the plan. Waiting with the C P U idle: a lock, or a slow downstream call. C P U high: profile the hot loop.

scenes.head: The method, in order
scenes.say: So the method. Confirm with metrics: p ninety nine, when it started, what changed. Locate with a trace. Explain with logs, tied together by a request id, and the query plan. Fix with one change. Verify the p ninety nine really dropped.

scenes.head: Buy time while you hunt
scenes.say: While you hunt, buy time. Roll back, if a deploy started it. Add a cache, if slow reads rarely change. Scale out, if load is the cause.

scenes.head: /checkout p99 after the index
scenes.say: We added the index. The p ninety nine falls from two thousand milliseconds to one fifty. Verified in the metrics, not guessed.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Design bit dot ly. Numbers first, base sixty two counter, database and cache. Why three oh two? Browsers cache three oh one, so you miss clicks. Analytics? Log clicks to a queue.
rows: log to a queue, count async

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Slow endpoint? Confirm with p ninety nine, trace, read the plan, fix, verify. Can't reproduce it? Use production traces and a request id. Mitigate? Roll back, cache, or scale.
rows: metrics, trace, logs/plan, fix one, verify
roll back, cache, or scale out

scenes.head: Build these next
scenes.say: Three exercises. Write encode and decode for base sixty two, and round trip a thousand ids. Size a service with fifty million posts a month. Run explain on your slowest query, add an index, and compare.
So say this. Do the numbers, encode a counter, cache reads, redirect with three oh two. In production, confirm with metrics, locate with a trace. Fix one thing, verify.
lines: Confirm with p99, locate with a trace.
Fix one thing, then verify the numbers.
